svg.text: How the chadgrant skills run a build, and where to look when it's slow
Top to bottom is the order things happen. Left: each step and who runs it. Right: what the step writes, and the journal events that record it.
Every subagent is a separate model session; each one's time grows with how much it reads, because every turn re-sends its whole context.
You ask for a feature, or say "spec this out"
Every question it can ask now, numbered, each with a recommended answer; it looks facts up itself.
You answer; it asks the next round until no decision is left assumed.
GLOSSARY first, then PRD, and ERD / DRD / API contract / UX / ops docs only where the work needs them.
Written by the main session itself, one doc after another, so every doc stays in its context.
Milestones (each a feature that ends in one review). Per milestone: its contracts (CON-###) first,
then tasks (TASK-###) that implement them: about 400 changed lines and one module each, never one per layer.
Each task: difficulty → tier, observe flag, hot files. Header: stack versions looked up, gates, max_parallel.
Why this stage feels slow: one session writes every document and the plan, and each later turn re-sends all of it.
Check: journal "turn" events (seconds, context, tool_calls) during planning.
Ask once: may Fable be used?
No answer means Opus for everything Hard. The answer is saved in the plan header and STATUS.md.
Stale (14 days or 50 commits)? A one-line reminder to you. It never starts a full review by itself.
One mid-tier agent writes "## Architecture" in AGENTS.md, about 60 lines: how screens mount, how routes and
sub-tabs register, where files live, hot files, test commands, worktree setup. The orchestrator reads and commits it.
One agent writes every contract for the milestone
Interfaces, abstract classes, protocols, shared types at their final paths; the doc comment is the spec
(behaviour, errors, invariants, an example); stubs that compile; contract tests that fail until implemented.
Against the milestone's REQs and the glossary; every task must have what it consumes. Then commit and freeze.
At most max_parallel tasks (default 4). Tasks depend only on contracts, so the cap sets the number of waves.
Reuse maps or batch discovery in a Fork. Each map: ≤40 lines with file ranges, reusable code, tests, and wiring.
Do trivial lookups directly. Pass the map in the brief; reference requirements already inherited by the worker.
3 · Dispatch the wave in one message
Brief: goal, REQs, CONs to implement and consume, the map, base commit, fast gate command, rules, report path.
Prefer Forks with worktree isolation; use non-fork workers when model, effort, or tool restrictions require it.
0 git merge --ff-only <base commit>; set up the worktree as the architecture note says
1 read the contracts, contract tests, architecture note, and the map; read line ranges, not whole files
2 contract tests red → green; then one test → code slice at a time for the rest
3 reuse first: search for existing code; Decorator for cross-cutting code; a dependency only at its latest stable release
4 fast gate: unit + contract tests, lint, types (never Docker); read its own diff once
5 report to .delivery/TASK-###.md; one line back: green|red, verify summary, ⚠, notes, contract changes
Never: commit, run Docker, edit a contract or a shared file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, STATUS.md, plan)
The orchestrator commits each green branch and merges it into the integration branch, in dependency order.
A conflict goes back to the worker that wrote it. Notes for shared docs are applied by the orchestrator.
5 · Fast gate on the merged tree
Green: drop the worktrees, next wave. Red: back to its worker; red again: a higher tier, a split task, or a fixed contract.
"Very small chunks"? Check dispatch brief_chars and how many tasks each wave has. "Workers slow"? Check agent
peak_context and first_edit_seconds: a high first edit means the map was thin.
git worktrees, one branch per task
merge commits on the integration branch
4 · Wave loop · until all tasks merged
The orchestrator alone starts Docker (if the project has it): integration tests, 90% coverage, e2e. Then stops it.
Failures become fix tasks at the owning task's tier, each in a fresh worktree.
chadgrant:code-review over the milestone diff, mid tier, ~45-minute budget. Nine lenses: spec, correctness, security,
tests, reuse, design, dependencies, Twelve-Factor, readability. Plus a top-tier security reviewer for observe tasks.
One fix pass, then the full gate again
Blockers and should-fix go back to the owning workers; nits are listed, not fixed. No second review.
Push · compact the docs · retro · STATUS.md · end the session
Compaction folds requirement changes into the docs; the retro turns repeated findings into lint rules or AGENTS.md lines.
A stale review stamp gets its one-line reminder here.
next milestone: a fresh session reads STATUS.md and starts at its contracts
Debugging: question → where to look (journal.py is in the plugin at skills/implementation/scripts/)
every event in order, with the gap before each
Are briefs too small or thin?
Did a change to the skills help?
